Warm orange background glow. A white speech bubble with black outline near the top. Inside the bubble the text reads: "Press the gas pedal. Ignore the engine. That's abstraction." Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes
panels.bubble_text: Press the gas pedal. Ignore the engine. That's abstraction.
panels.speaker: SPROUT

panels.text: Every layer in the computing stack does the same thing the gas pedal does: it hides overwhelming complexity and exposes a simple interface.

panels.prompt: A warm split-screen triptych showing three moments of computing abstraction history: on the left, a woman in 1950s naval uniform at a room-sized computer writing on paper (Grace Hopper and the compiler, 1952); in the center, two young bearded men at a PDP-11 terminal in a cluttered 1969 office (Thompson and Ritchie building Unix); on the right, a modern Google conference room with researchers presenting a paper, a whiteboard showing 'Attention Is All You Need' (Vaswani et al., 2017). Each scene softly glows with its era's accent color. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes

panels.text:
When Grace Hopper built the first compiler in 1952, she created an abstraction. When Thompson and Ritchie built Unix in 1969, they created an abstraction. When Vaswani and colleagues published the Transformer in 2017, they created an abstraction.

Each abstraction is an act of trust. You trust that the layer below you works correctly. And mostly, that trust is justified. But not always.

panels.prompt: A small cute origami-style robot made of folded paper with dot-matrix eyes, shaped like a tiny filing cabinet with stubby paper legs and arms, holding a magnifying glass up to a cracked glowing pipe that is leaking sparks and binary digits. Water droplets of code dripping from the cracks. Warm orange accent lighting. A white speech bubble with black outline near the top. Inside the bubble the text reads: "Sometimes the layers below you leak through." Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes
panels.bubble_text: Sometimes the layers below you leak through.
panels.speaker: TAPE

panels.text: In 2002, Joel Spolsky coined "The Law of Leaky Abstractions": all non-trivial abstractions, to some degree, are leaky. A performance problem in your AI agent traces back to GPU architecture. A security vulnerability traces back to memory management in C.

Grace Hopper used to hand out 11.8-inch pieces of wire to admirals — representing the distance light travels in one nanosecond — to explain why satellite communication was slow. Understanding the full stack gives you diagnostic superpowers. When something breaks, you know where to look.

panels.prompt: A small cute round rust-orange robot with a dome head and big knowing amber LED eyes, stubby arms holding a bucket with water leaking through tiny holes, each leak labeled LATENCY MEMORY BUGS, antenna with a tiny drip on top. A white speech bubble with black outline above. Inside the bubble the text reads: "All abstractions leak. The trick is knowing where." Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes
panels.bubble_text: All abstractions leak. The trick is knowing where.
panels.speaker: LEAKBOT

panels.text: Can you think of other abstractions in daily life? A light switch hides the power grid. A restaurant menu hides the kitchen. Money hides a complex web of trust and accounting. Abstractions are everywhere — computing just made them the foundation of an entire technology stack.

panels.lab_description: Ride between all 8 floors of computing — each one has an interactive demo. Toggle a transistor. Wire a logic gate. Watch a swarm race. See abstraction in action.

panels.text: Abstraction is not simplification. Simplification throws away detail. Abstraction HIDES detail behind a clean interface while keeping all the power underneath. It lets you be "absolutely precise" (Dijkstra) at your own level without drowning in every level below.

We have seen the stack. We have understood its superpower. Now let's walk through the people who built it — every key figure from all nine previous issues — and see how their work connects into a single story.
